doc.title: Putter Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 27, 2024

title: The good old days, synthesizers and the state of jazz
summary: Asked about the good old days, Smith says old men always say that, tells of buying an early synthesizer in Japan, and says jazz improvisers are still evolving.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That’s fine. Just to wrap up, are you a person who thinks about the good old days, that reminisces and thinks that things now are not nearly as positive as they used to be?

Oh of course. Of course. I’m an old man. I mean that’s the birthright of old men you know. I read this thing that said that young people today have no respect for their elders, they have no respect for like traditional ways and politeness and, I’m paraphrasing, and on and on, and it was a speech made by Cicero 2500 years ago. So there you go.
Well musically when, I don’t know if this is answerable, but musically when did the good old days start to pass?

I guess I’m thinking some of the musicians I’ve talked to, studio guys, they talk about this bit, some of them will be dramatic about it. “I can remember when we went to A&M Studios and we saw the first synthesizer.” As if that was like an alarm bell going off.
That was a what going on?
Like an alarm bell, like we’ve seen the future and we don’t like it.

No I was in Japan and saw it there before it was here and I bought one. It was $1,100. And it was like oh my God this is great, there was no kind of an alarm bell. I brought it home and I was programming Bach fugues on it and stuff like that you know. Because you could do it one note at a time. Because I’m not a piano player you know. And somebody came over and I said, “Listen to this.” And I turned it on and said, “I did this.” You know? “My God, I didn’t know you played piano.” So it was like a great tool but the recording industry is a whole different line of work. It’s like rock & roll and then there’s pop stuff and I mean stuff like Johnny Mathis and Tony Bennett quality, Frank Sinatra. And I guess I listened — just the other day I listened, just because — Taylor Swift, you know I listened to her thing and it was like well that didn’t bother me you know. I mean it didn’t bother me. And it wasn’t like Mick Jagger. That bothers me. But I mean I feel like we’re people that — I hate to use the word “real jazz” but people that are devoted to improvising and that’s evolving and it’s been evolving. It’s just going on and it’s a great art form and there are thousands of young people involved in this art form. And as to how many of them will last, but the good old days, I don’t know it’s always like when you’re 20 you go, “Oh yeah man, I missed out on the good old days,” you know. days were the last ten years you know. So maybe the good old days is always the old days you know. Geez remember back in 2009, remember back then? Gee I don’t know.
I can’t remember what I had for dinner last night. I mean I’m getting to the age where certain old things that were funny are now crude like. I’ve forgotten more than you’ll ever know.
